Chapter 6  ·  CS229 Machine Learning

The Exponential Family
and Generalized Linear Models

A unified framework that explains why linear and logistic regression are two faces of the same coin — and how to build principled models for any type of output.

Learning Objectives

  • Define the exponential family form $p(y;\eta) = b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta))$ and identify its components: base measure, sufficient statistic, natural parameter, and log-partition function.
  • Derive exponential family representations of the Bernoulli and Gaussian distributions through algebraic pattern-matching.
  • Prove the moment properties $\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]=a'(\eta)$ and $\mathrm{Var}[y;\eta]=a''(\eta)$ by differentiating the normalization identity.
  • Explain exponential tilting as the constructive origin of the exponential family and interpret $a(\eta)$ as a log moment-generating function.
  • State and apply the three GLM assumptions to derive a model hypothesis $h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x)$ for any chosen exponential family.
  • Identify the canonical response function $g$ and canonical link $g^{-1}$ for the Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson families.
  • Derive ordinary least squares and logistic regression as GLMs from the Gaussian and Bernoulli exponential families.
  • Construct a Poisson GLM for count data and interpret its log-linear hypothesis function.
  • Apply and prove the universal GLM gradient update $\theta := \theta + \alpha(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)}))x^{(i)}$ for all exponential families.
  • Derive the softmax model as the categorical GLM and interpret it geometrically as one parameter vector per class.

6.1 The Exponential Family

So far in this course we have encountered two supervised learning models: linear regression for real-valued outputs and logistic regression for binary labels. In both cases we wrote down a probabilistic interpretation and derived a learning algorithm from it. A surprising fact is that these two models, which look quite different on the surface, are special cases of a single unifying framework called Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). The key ingredient that makes this unification possible is the exponential family of distributions.

The exponential family is not one distribution but an entire class sharing a common algebraic form. It includes the Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, gamma, exponential, beta, Dirichlet, and many others. When you choose a distribution from this family and combine it with a linear predictor through three specific modeling assumptions, you are guaranteed to obtain a valid probabilistic model with a convex log-likelihood and a universal gradient update rule. This chapter develops that theory from first principles.

We begin with the formal definition of the exponential family form and then examine the constructive process — exponential tilting — that reveals intuitively where this form originates.

6.1.1 The Canonical Form

A probability distribution belongs to the exponential family if its probability density function (pdf) or probability mass function (pmf) can be written in a specific canonical form. The governing parameter is called the natural parameter, denoted $\eta$.

Definition · Exponential Family

A family of distributions indexed by $\eta \in \mathbb{R}^k$ belongs to the exponential family if its pdf or pmf can be written as $$p(y;\eta) = b(y)\exp\!\bigl(\eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta)\bigr),$$ where:

  • $y$ is the data (the random variable),
  • $\eta \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is the natural parameter (canonical parameter),
  • $T(y) \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is the sufficient statistic; for nearly all models in this course, $T(y)=y$,
  • $b(y) \geq 0$ is the base measure, depending only on $y$, and
  • $a(\eta)$ is the log-partition function, determined entirely by $b$ and $T$ via $$a(\eta) = \log\int b(y)\exp\!\bigl(\eta^\top T(y)\bigr)\,dy.$$

The log-partition function $a(\eta)$ is not a free design choice — it is the logarithm of the normalizing integral and is therefore completely determined once $b$ and $T$ are chosen. As $\eta$ varies, $a(\eta)$ adjusts to keep the distribution normalized. This enforced relationship between $a$ and the rest of the distribution is what gives the exponential family its remarkable properties.

Intuition · The Log-Partition Function

Think of $a(\eta)$ as the "price of normalization." You define an unnormalized density $b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y))$. The total mass of this function over all $y$ is some positive number $Z(\eta)$. To make it a valid probability distribution you divide by $Z(\eta)$, or equivalently subtract $\log Z(\eta) = a(\eta)$ from the exponent. Because $a$ depends on $\eta$, the cost of normalization changes as the parameter moves — and as we will see in Section 6.3, the way $a$ changes with $\eta$ encodes all the moments of the distribution.

6.1.2 Exponential Tilting: Where the Family Comes From

To understand why the exponential family takes this particular form, consider the following constructive process. Begin with any non-negative function $b(y)$ that integrates to a finite positive constant. Now introduce a parameter $\eta$ and define a new distribution by multiplying $b(y)$ by the factor $e^{\eta y}$ (scalar case, $T(y)=y$), then renormalizing:

$$p(y;\eta) = \frac{b(y)\,e^{\eta y}}{\displaystyle\int b(y')e^{\eta y'}\,dy'} = b(y)\exp\!\Bigl(\eta y - \log\textstyle\int b(y')e^{\eta y'}\,dy'\Bigr).$$

The denominator's logarithm is precisely $a(\eta)$, so this is an exponential family distribution. This operation is called exponential tilting: multiplying $b(y)$ by $e^{\eta y}$ "tilts" its probability mass. For $\eta > 0$ the exponential factor is increasing, lifting the right tail; for $\eta < 0$ it lifts the left tail. The renormalization preserves the total probability mass at 1. Figure 6.1 illustrates this process using a Gaussian base measure.

Figure 6.1. Exponential tilting of a Gaussian base measure $b(y) = \mathcal{N}(y;0,1.5^2)$ (left panel). The right panel shows the resulting tilted distributions for $\eta \in \{-1.5, 0, 1.5\}$ (red, blue, green). Larger $\eta$ shifts mass rightward; $\eta=0$ recovers the base measure after renormalization. The family remains Gaussian under tilting, illustrating closure: the Gaussian exponential family is closed under its own tilting operation.

There is a connection to moment-generating functions (MGFs) worth noting. The denominator of the tilted distribution is $e^{a(\eta)} = \int b(y)e^{\eta y}\,dy = \mathbb{E}_{b}[e^{\eta y}]$, which is exactly the MGF of the base measure evaluated at $\eta$. This is why differentiating $a(\eta)$ generates the moments of the distribution — a key property we develop carefully in Section 6.3.

💡
Key insight: The exponential family is the unique family that arises when you want to parameterize distributions by "tilting" a base measure in the direction of a sufficient statistic $T(y)$. The parameter $\eta$ controls the tilt direction and magnitude; $a(\eta)$ tracks the normalizing cost.

6.2 Bernoulli and Gaussian as Exponential Family Members

The claim that the exponential family is a unifying framework requires substantiation. We need to show that the specific distributions we have used — Bernoulli and Gaussian — do in fact belong to this family. We do this by starting from the standard parametric form of each distribution and algebraically massaging it into the canonical exponential family form $b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta))$, then using pattern-matching to identify the four components.

This exercise is not mere verification. The Bernoulli derivation reveals something deep: the logistic sigmoid function, which we previously introduced as a convenient squashing function for classification, emerges necessarily from the Bernoulli exponential family representation. It is not a design choice — it is forced upon us by the structure of the Bernoulli distribution and the requirement that the natural parameter be real-valued.

6.2.1 The Bernoulli Distribution

Recall that the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $\phi \in (0,1)$ has pmf $p(y;\phi) = \phi^y(1-\phi)^{1-y}$ for $y \in \{0,1\}$. We now derive its exponential family representation.

Theorem · Bernoulli Exponential Family

The Bernoulli distribution with mean parameter $\phi \in (0,1)$ belongs to the exponential family with:

  • Natural parameter: $\eta = \log\dfrac{\phi}{1-\phi}$
  • Sufficient statistic: $T(y) = y$
  • Log-partition function: $a(\eta) = \log(1 + e^\eta)$
  • Base measure: $b(y) = 1$

Inverting, $\phi = \sigma(\eta) := 1/(1+e^{-\eta})$, the logistic sigmoid function.

Proof

Starting from $p(y;\phi) = \phi^y(1-\phi)^{1-y}$, write this as the exponential of its own logarithm:

$$p(y;\phi) = \exp\bigl(y\log\phi + (1-y)\log(1-\phi)\bigr).$$

Collect the terms in $y$ to the left and the remaining term to the right:

$$= \exp\!\Bigl(y\underbrace{\log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}}_{\eta} + \log(1-\phi)\Bigr).$$

We identify $\eta = \log(\phi/(1-\phi))$. Solving for $\phi$: $e^\eta = \phi/(1-\phi)$, so $\phi = e^\eta/(1+e^\eta) = 1/(1+e^{-\eta}) = \sigma(\eta)$. Substituting into $\log(1-\phi)$:

$$\log(1-\sigma(\eta)) = \log\frac{1}{1+e^\eta} = -\log(1+e^\eta) = -a(\eta).$$

Therefore $p(y;\eta) = 1\cdot\exp(\eta y - \log(1+e^\eta))$, confirming $b(y)=1$, $T(y)=y$, $a(\eta)=\log(1+e^\eta)$. □

Figure 6.2. Left: the canonical response function $g(\eta)=\sigma(\eta)=(1+e^{-\eta})^{-1}$ maps the natural parameter $\eta$ to the mean parameter $\phi$. The red dashed line marks $\phi=0.5$ (the decision boundary where $\eta=0$). Right: the log-partition function $a(\eta)=\log(1+e^\eta)$ (green) and its first derivative $a'(\eta)=\phi=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (gold dashed). The softness of the step reflects maximum uncertainty near $\eta=0$ and confident classification for large $|\eta|$.
Example · Verifying Normalization

Setup: We verify that $a(\eta) = \log(1+e^\eta)$ is indeed the correct log-partition function for the Bernoulli distribution expressed in natural-parameter form.

Derivation: Normalization requires $p(0;\eta) + p(1;\eta) = 1$:

$$e^{0 - a(\eta)} + e^{\eta - a(\eta)} = e^{-a(\eta)}(1 + e^\eta) = 1 \implies a(\eta) = \log(1+e^\eta). \quad\checkmark$$

Conclusion: The sigmoid $\sigma(\eta)$ is uniquely determined by requiring the Bernoulli pmf to normalize over $y \in \{0,1\}$. It emerges from the structure of the problem, not from a heuristic choice.

Warning · Confusing $\phi$ with $\eta$

The Bernoulli distribution has two different parametrizations: the mean parameter $\phi \in (0,1)$ and the natural parameter $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$, related by $\phi = \sigma(\eta)$. When building GLMs (Section 6.4), the natural parameter is set to $\eta = \theta^\top x$, which can be any real number — consistent with $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$. If you mistakenly set $\phi = \theta^\top x$ directly, predictions may lie outside $(0,1)$, yielding a nonsensical probability. Always work with the natural parameter when applying the GLM framework.

6.2.2 The Gaussian Distribution

We now perform the same pattern-matching exercise for the Gaussian distribution. For GLM purposes we treat the variance $\sigma^2$ as a fixed known constant and derive the exponential family representation in terms of the mean $\mu$. Setting $\sigma^2 = 1$ simplifies algebra without loss of generality: any fixed $\sigma^2$ introduces only a constant scale factor that does not affect the structure of the GLM hypothesis.

Theorem · Gaussian Exponential Family ($\sigma^2 = 1$)

The Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ belongs to the exponential family with:

  • Natural parameter: $\eta = \mu$
  • Sufficient statistic: $T(y) = y$
  • Log-partition function: $a(\eta) = \eta^2/2$
  • Base measure: $b(y) = (2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-y^2/2)$

The canonical response function is the identity: $g(\eta) = \eta$, so $\mu = \eta$.

Proof

Starting from $p(y;\mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\bigl(-\frac{1}{2}(y-\mu)^2\bigr)$, expand the square $(y-\mu)^2 = y^2 - 2\mu y + \mu^2$:

$$p(y;\mu) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2/2}}_{b(y)} \cdot \exp\!\Bigl(\underbrace{\mu}_{\eta}\cdot y - \underbrace{\frac{\mu^2}{2}}_{a(\eta)}\Bigr).$$

Pattern-matching gives $b(y) = (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-y^2/2}$, $T(y)=y$, $\eta=\mu$, $a(\eta)=\eta^2/2$. Since the canonical response is $g(\eta) = a'(\eta) = \eta$, the Gaussian has the identity response function. □

Figure 6.3. Left: Gaussian pdfs $\mathcal{N}(\mu,1)$ for $\mu \in \{-2, 0, 2\}$ (red, dark-navy, green). Varying the natural parameter $\eta = \mu$ simply translates the distribution. Right: the log-partition function $a(\eta)=\eta^2/2$ (blue), its first derivative $a'(\eta)=\eta=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (gold dashed), and second derivative $a''(\eta)=1=\mathrm{Var}[Y]$ (green dotted). The constant second derivative reflects that a unit-variance Gaussian has the same spread regardless of its mean.
Data Science Application · Choosing a Distribution by Output Type

In practice, choosing the exponential family distribution is guided by the data type of the output variable $y$:

Data type of $y$SupportDistributionModel name
Real-valued$(-\infty,+\infty)$GaussianLinear regression
Binary$\{0,1\}$BernoulliLogistic regression
Counts$\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$PoissonPoisson / count regression
Multi-class$\{1,\ldots,k\}$CategoricalSoftmax regression
Positive real$(0,\infty)$Gamma / ExponentialSurvival analysis

This table is your first reference when designing a new model. Choose the distribution whose support matches the range of $y$; the rest of the GLM construction follows mechanically from the exponential family representation.

6.3 Properties of the Exponential Family

The exponential family is more than a convenient algebraic form. It carries deep structural properties that make computation tractable, estimation principled, and the geometry of statistical inference transparent. The two most important properties concern how the moments of the distribution relate to the log-partition function $a(\eta)$, and what this implies for the maximum likelihood problem.

These properties flow directly from the connection between $a(\eta)$ and the moment-generating function of $T(y)$. Recall that $e^{a(\eta)} = \int b(y)e^{\eta T(y)}\,dy = \mathbb{E}_b[e^{\eta T(y)}]$, the MGF of $T(y)$ under the base measure $b$. Differentiating an MGF at a point generates the moments at that point. That is exactly what we exploit here.

6.3.1 Moments from the Log-Partition Function

Theorem · Moment-Generating Properties of $a(\eta)$

For an exponential family distribution $p(y;\eta) = b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta))$, assuming regularity conditions permitting differentiation under the integral sign:

$$\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta] = \nabla_\eta a(\eta), \qquad \mathrm{Var}[T(y);\eta] = \nabla^2_\eta a(\eta).$$

In the scalar case with $T(y)=y$:

$$\mathbb{E}[y;\eta] = a'(\eta), \qquad \mathrm{Var}[y;\eta] = a''(\eta).$$
Proof

Since $p(y;\eta)$ is a valid pdf, $\int b(y)\exp(\eta T(y) - a(\eta))\,dy = 1$ for all $\eta$. Differentiate both sides with respect to $\eta$ (using Leibniz rule, valid under regularity):

$$\int b(y)\bigl(T(y) - a'(\eta)\bigr)\exp(\eta T(y)-a(\eta))\,dy = 0.$$

Splitting and recognizing $\int T(y)p(y;\eta)\,dy = \mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta]$:

$$\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta] - a'(\eta) = 0 \implies \boxed{\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta] = a'(\eta)}.$$

For the variance, differentiate the identity $\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta] = a'(\eta)$ again with respect to $\eta$. The left side differentiates as $\mathbb{E}[T(y)^2;\eta] - (\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta])^2$ (the derivative of an expectation), and the right side as $a''(\eta)$:

$$\mathbb{E}[T(y)^2] - (\mathbb{E}[T(y)])^2 = a''(\eta) \implies \boxed{\mathrm{Var}[T(y);\eta] = a''(\eta).} \qquad \square$$
Core Result
$$\mathbb{E}[y;\eta] = a'(\eta) \qquad\qquad \mathrm{Var}[y;\eta] = a''(\eta)$$

This is a remarkable result. Computing moments ordinarily requires integrating $y \cdot p(y;\eta)$ and $y^2 \cdot p(y;\eta)$ over all $y$ — integrals that can be difficult. For exponential family distributions, these integrals reduce to derivatives of $a$, which are typically straightforward calculus.

Example · Moments of Bernoulli and Gaussian via $a(\eta)$

Bernoulli: $a(\eta) = \log(1+e^\eta)$. Then: $$a'(\eta) = \frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta} = \sigma(\eta) = \phi = \mathbb{E}[y]. \quad\checkmark$$ $$a''(\eta) = \sigma(\eta)(1-\sigma(\eta)) = \phi(1-\phi) = \mathrm{Var}[y]. \quad\checkmark$$

Gaussian ($\sigma^2=1$): $a(\eta) = \eta^2/2$. Then: $$a'(\eta) = \eta = \mu = \mathbb{E}[y]. \quad\checkmark \qquad a''(\eta) = 1 = \mathrm{Var}[y]. \quad\checkmark$$

Takeaway: In both cases, differentiation of $a$ reproduces the well-known moments without any direct integration. The log-partition function "encodes" the entire moment sequence of the distribution.

Figure 6.7. Left: for the Gaussian family, $a(\eta)=\eta^2/2$ (blue), $a'(\eta)=\eta=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (gold dashed), and the shaded band illustrates the constant $a''(\eta)=\mathrm{Var}[Y]=1$. Right: for the Bernoulli family, $a(\eta)=\log(1+e^\eta)$ (blue), $a'(\eta)=\phi=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (gold dashed), and $a''(\eta)=\phi(1-\phi)=\mathrm{Var}[Y]$ (green dotted). The variance peaks at $\eta=0$ where the Bernoulli distribution is most uncertain ($\phi=0.5$) and tends to zero for large $|\eta|$ where the distribution becomes deterministic.

6.3.2 Concavity and the MLE

A practically important consequence of the exponential family structure is that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a convex optimization problem in the natural parameter $\eta$. This is a strong guarantee: gradient descent on the negative log-likelihood will always find the unique global minimum, with no risk of being trapped in local minima.

Theorem · Concavity of the Log-Likelihood

For any exponential family distribution, the log-likelihood $\ell(\eta) = \log p(y;\eta)$ is concave in $\eta$. Equivalently, the negative log-likelihood (the loss function for MLE) is convex in $\eta$.

Proof Sketch

The log-likelihood for a single observation is $\ell(\eta) = \log b(y) + \eta^\top T(y) - a(\eta)$. The term $\log b(y)$ is constant in $\eta$; the term $\eta^\top T(y)$ is linear in $\eta$ (hence concave). The only non-linear term is $-a(\eta)$. By the variance theorem, $\nabla^2 a(\eta) = \mathrm{Var}[T(y);\eta] \succeq 0$, so $a(\eta)$ is convex. Therefore $-a(\eta)$ is concave, and the sum of a linear and a concave function is concave. □

Intuition · Why Convexity Follows from Variance

The curvature of $a(\eta)$ equals the variance of $T(y)$, which is always non-negative. This means $a$ can only curve upward (convex), never downward. The log-likelihood is $\ell = \text{linear} - a$, so its curvature is $-a''(\eta) = -\mathrm{Var} \leq 0$: it always curves downward (concave). A concave function has a unique global maximum — the MLE is always well-defined and gradient ascent always finds it.

📖
Connection to CS229 HW: The homework asks you to prove these two properties rigorously. The key steps are: (1) differentiate the normalization identity $\int p(y;\eta)\,dy = 1$ twice with respect to $\eta$; (2) interpret the resulting equations as the mean and variance of $T(y)$. The proof template used above is the standard approach.

6.4 Generalized Linear Models

We now arrive at the central application of the exponential family theory. In supervised learning, we are given input-output pairs $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ and want to model the conditional distribution of $y$ given $x$. Previously, linear regression modeled $y|x \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta^\top x, \sigma^2)$ and logistic regression modeled $y|x \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(\theta^\top x))$. These were derived somewhat separately. Generalized Linear Models provide a single principled framework that subsumes both — and extends to any exponential family distribution.

The connecting idea is to link the natural parameter $\eta$ of an exponential family distribution to the input features $x$ through a linear map $\theta^\top x$. The model is called "linear" because $\theta^\top x$ is linear in $\theta$, and "generalized" because the output $y$ can follow any exponential family distribution, not just the Gaussian.

6.4.1 The Three GLM Assumptions

Definition · Generalized Linear Model (GLM)

Given features $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a GLM is defined by three assumptions:

  1. Exponential family: $y \mid x;\theta \sim \mathrm{ExponentialFamily}(\eta)$. Conditioned on $x$ and $\theta$, the output follows an exponential family distribution with natural parameter $\eta$.
  2. Mean prediction: The hypothesis predicts the conditional mean: $h_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid x;\theta]$.
  3. Linearity: The natural parameter is the linear predictor: $\eta = \theta^\top x$.

Together these force $h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x)$ where $g(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ is the canonical response function.

The derivation of the hypothesis function follows immediately. From assumption 3, $\eta = \theta^\top x$. From assumption 2, we want $h_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$. From Section 6.3, $\mathbb{E}[y;\eta] = a'(\eta) = g(\eta)$. Combining:

GLM Hypothesis
$$h_\theta(x) \;=\; g(\theta^\top x) \;=\; \mathbb{E}[y \mid x;\theta]$$

The data-generation pipeline for a GLM can be visualized as a three-stage process: $$x^{(i)} \;\xrightarrow{\;\theta^\top\;} \;\eta^{(i)} = \theta^\top x^{(i)} \;\xrightarrow{\;g\;} \;\mu^{(i)} = g(\eta^{(i)}) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{sample}\;} \;y^{(i)} \sim p(y;\eta^{(i)}).$$ The parameter $\theta$ is global — shared across all examples. The natural parameter $\eta^{(i)}$ is per-example, computed fresh from each input $x^{(i)}$. The output $y^{(i)}$ is sampled from the exponential family distribution with that natural parameter.

6.4.2 Canonical Response and Link Functions

The function $g$ mapping the natural parameter to the mean is called the canonical response function. It is entirely determined by the choice of exponential family — it is $g(\eta) = a'(\eta)$. Its inverse $g^{-1}$ is called the canonical link function, mapping the mean back to the natural parameter. Both are always well-defined because $a''(\eta) = \mathrm{Var}[y;\eta] > 0$ (for non-degenerate distributions) implies $a'$ is strictly monotone, hence invertible.

Definition · Canonical Response and Link Functions

For an exponential family with log-partition $a$:

  • The canonical response function is $g(\eta) = a'(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$, mapping $\mathbb{R} \to \mathrm{range}(\mathbb{E}[y])$.
  • The canonical link function is $g^{-1}: \mathrm{range}(\mathbb{E}[y]) \to \mathbb{R}$, the inverse of $g$.

Key instances: $g(\eta)=\eta$ (Gaussian), $g(\eta)=\sigma(\eta)$ (Bernoulli), $g(\eta)=e^\eta$ (Poisson).

Figure 6.5. Canonical response functions $g(\eta)$ for three exponential families: the identity (Gaussian, blue), the logistic sigmoid (Bernoulli, green), and the exponential (Poisson, gold). Each maps the unrestricted natural parameter $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$ to the valid range of the corresponding mean parameter. The Gaussian mean is unconstrained; the Bernoulli mean must lie in $(0,1)$; the Poisson mean must be positive. The canonical response function automatically enforces these constraints.

6.4.3 OLS and Logistic Regression as GLMs

We can now recover linear regression and logistic regression as special cases of the GLM framework by choosing the Gaussian and Bernoulli families, respectively. This reframes results from earlier chapters as consequences of a unified theory rather than separate derivations.

Example · Linear Regression as a Gaussian GLM

Setup: Choose $y \mid x;\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,1)$ (Gaussian family, $\sigma^2=1$).

Derivation: From Section 6.2.2, $\eta = \mu$ and $g(\eta) = \eta$ (identity). Setting $\eta = \theta^\top x$: $$h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x) = \theta^\top x.$$

Result: The Gaussian GLM exactly reproduces ordinary least squares linear regression. The squared loss $\|y - \theta^\top x\|^2$ emerges from maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood.

Example · Logistic Regression as a Bernoulli GLM

Setup: Choose $y \mid x;\theta \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\phi)$ (Bernoulli family).

Derivation: From Section 6.2.1, $\eta = \log(\phi/(1-\phi))$ and $g(\eta) = \sigma(\eta)$. Setting $\eta = \theta^\top x$: $$h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x) = \sigma(\theta^\top x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^\top x}}.$$

Result: The Bernoulli GLM exactly reproduces logistic regression. The sigmoid activation is not a heuristic squashing function — it is the canonical response function of the Bernoulli exponential family, forced upon us by the mathematics.

Figure 6.4. Left: linear regression GLM. The navy line shows $\mu(x)=\theta x$ ($\theta=1$); blue dots are observations sampled from $\mathcal{N}(\theta x^{(i)}, 0.64)$; gold overlays show Gaussian densities at $x \in \{-2,0,2\}$. Right: logistic regression GLM. The navy sigmoid shows $\phi(x)=\sigma(\theta x)$; blue dots are $y=1$ observations, red are $y=0$; gold dashed marks the $\phi=0.5$ decision boundary. In both panels the learning task is to recover the true $\theta$ from the noisy observations.
💡
Key insight: The sigmoid in logistic regression is not a design choice — it is the unique function forced by requiring $y$ to be Bernoulli-distributed and the natural parameter to be linear in $x$. This gives logistic regression a principled probabilistic justification that the original formulation did not make explicit.

6.5 Other GLMs: Poisson Regression and Beyond

The GLM framework extends far beyond the Gaussian and Bernoulli families. Whenever the output variable $y$ has a data type incompatible with the Gaussian (which has support $\mathbb{R}$), we should choose a different exponential family. A canonical practical example is count data: $y \in \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ representing non-negative integer quantities like number of customer arrivals per hour, number of transactions in a time window, or number of defects in a product. The natural exponential family distribution for counts is the Poisson.

The workflow is always the same: (1) identify the data type of $y$, (2) choose a compatible exponential family distribution, (3) derive its exponential family representation to find $\eta$, $a(\eta)$, and $g(\eta)$, (4) write $h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x)$, and (5) apply the universal gradient update rule. The GLM framework transforms what would be many separate derivations into one reusable pipeline.

6.5.1 Poisson Regression for Count Data

The Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda > 0$ assigns probability $p(y;\lambda) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y/y!$ to count $y \in \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Its mean and variance are both equal to $\lambda$, a special property called equidispersion.

Theorem · Poisson Exponential Family

The Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda > 0$ belongs to the exponential family with:

  • Natural parameter: $\eta = \log\lambda$
  • Sufficient statistic: $T(y) = y$
  • Log-partition function: $a(\eta) = e^\eta$
  • Base measure: $b(y) = 1/y!$

The canonical response is $g(\eta) = e^\eta$ and the canonical link is $g^{-1}(\mu) = \log\mu$.

Proof

From $p(y;\lambda) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y/y!$, substitute $\lambda = e^\eta$ (valid since $\lambda > 0 \Leftrightarrow \eta \in \mathbb{R}$):

$$p(y;\eta) = \frac{e^{-e^\eta}(e^\eta)^y}{y!} = \frac{1}{y!}\exp(\eta y - e^\eta).$$

Pattern-matching: $b(y)=1/y!$, $T(y)=y$, $\eta=\log\lambda$, $a(\eta)=e^\eta$.

Verification: $a'(\eta) = e^\eta = \lambda = \mathbb{E}[y]$ ✓ and $a''(\eta) = e^\eta = \lambda = \mathrm{Var}[y]$ ✓. □

Example · Poisson GLM for Web Traffic Prediction

Setup: We wish to model the number of user logins $y$ per hour as a function of features $x$ such as time of day, day of week, and marketing spend.

Derivation: Apply the three GLM assumptions with the Poisson family. The canonical response is $g(\eta) = e^\eta$. Setting $\eta = \theta^\top x$: $$h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x) = e^{\theta^\top x}.$$

Result: The Poisson GLM predicts $\hat{y} = e^{\theta^\top x}$, which is always positive — consistent with count data. Taking logs, $\log \hat{y} = \theta^\top x$, so the model is linear in log-space. This is why Poisson regression is sometimes called a log-linear model. The feature coefficient $\theta_j$ measures the multiplicative change in predicted count per unit change in $x_j$: increasing $x_j$ by 1 multiplies $\hat{y}$ by $e^{\theta_j}$.

Warning · Overdispersion in Count Data

The Poisson distribution forces $\mathbb{E}[y] = \mathrm{Var}[y] = \lambda$. Real count data often exhibits overdispersion: $\mathrm{Var}[y] > \mathbb{E}[y]$. When this happens, the Poisson log-likelihood is misspecified, standard errors are underestimated, and hypothesis tests are anti-conservative. A diagnostic is to check whether the sample variance of the counts substantially exceeds the sample mean. If overdispersion is present, the negative binomial distribution (which adds a separate dispersion parameter) is a more flexible alternative, though it falls outside the strict exponential family unless the dispersion is held fixed.

6.5.2 The Universal GLM Gradient Update Rule

One of the most elegant consequences of the GLM framework is that maximum likelihood estimation leads to the same gradient update rule for every exponential family choice. You derive it once, and it applies to all GLMs — including Poisson, gamma, and any distribution you might invent.

Theorem · Universal GLM Gradient Update

For any GLM with exponential family distribution, the stochastic gradient ascent update on the log-likelihood with respect to the model parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is:

$$\theta_j := \theta_j + \alpha\bigl(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)})\bigr)x_j^{(i)}, \qquad j = 1,\ldots,d.$$

Here $\alpha > 0$ is the learning rate and $h_\theta(x^{(i)}) = g(\theta^\top x^{(i)}) = \mathbb{E}[y^{(i)}|x^{(i)};\theta]$ is the predicted mean. This form holds for every exponential family choice.

Proof

The log-likelihood for one example, viewed as a function of $\theta$, is $\ell(\theta) = \log b(y^{(i)}) + \eta T(y^{(i)}) - a(\eta)$ where $\eta = \theta^\top x^{(i)}$. Taking the partial derivative with respect to $\theta_j$ via the chain rule:

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_j} = \bigl(T(y^{(i)}) - a'(\eta)\bigr) \cdot \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial \theta_j} = \bigl(y^{(i)} - \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]\bigr) \cdot x_j^{(i)} = \bigl(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)})\bigr)x_j^{(i)}.$$

We used $T(y)=y$, $a'(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]=h_\theta(x^{(i)})$, and $\partial\eta/\partial\theta_j = x_j^{(i)}$. The gradient ascent update $\theta_j := \theta_j + \alpha\,\partial\ell/\partial\theta_j$ gives the stated rule. □

Data Science Application · One Update Rule Across All Models

The universality of the update rule has direct practical implications. In PyTorch or TensorFlow, when you use cross-entropy loss for classification or mean-squared error for regression, the gradient that backpropagates through the final linear layer is always of the form $(y - \hat{y})\cdot x$. For linear regression: $y^{(i)} - \theta^\top x^{(i)}$ (residual). For logistic regression: $y^{(i)} - \sigma(\theta^\top x^{(i)})$ (probability error). For Poisson regression: $y^{(i)} - e^{\theta^\top x^{(i)}}$ (count error). The error signal is always "observed minus predicted mean" — a direct consequence of the exponential family moment property $a'(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$.

6.6 Softmax Regression

All GLMs considered so far have scalar or binary outputs. Many real-world tasks require predicting one of $k > 2$ discrete classes: the digit in an image, the sentiment of a review (positive/neutral/negative), the topic of a news article, or the language of a text. This is the multi-class classification problem, and the GLM for it is softmax regression, also called multinomial logistic regression.

The appropriate exponential family for multi-class output $y \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ is the categorical distribution. Unlike Bernoulli (one free parameter $\phi$), the categorical distribution over $k$ classes has $k-1$ free parameters. The GLM construction therefore requires one parameter vector $\theta_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$ per class, collected into a matrix $\Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$. The resulting hypothesis function is the softmax transformation.

6.6.1 The Categorical Distribution and the Softmax Function

Definition · Softmax Function and Softmax Regression

The softmax function converts a vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^k$ of real-valued scores into a probability vector:

$$\mathrm{softmax}(z)_j = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^k e^{z_\ell}}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,k.$$

For softmax regression with per-class parameters $\theta_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the predicted class probabilities are:

$$p(y=j \mid x;\Theta) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j^\top x)}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^k \exp(\theta_\ell^\top x)}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,k,$$

where $\Theta = [\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k] \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ collects all parameters. The predicted class is $\hat{y} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_j \,\theta_j^\top x$.

Intuition · Why Exponentiate and Renormalize?

Given raw scores $z_j = \theta_j^\top x$ (one per class, any real number), we need non-negative numbers that sum to 1. Exponentiation $e^{z_j}$ converts any real score to a positive number while preserving order: $z_i > z_j \Rightarrow e^{z_i} > e^{z_j}$. Dividing by $\sum_\ell e^{z_\ell}$ renormalizes. As the score gap $z_i - z_j \to \infty$, all probability concentrates on the leading class: softmax approximates a hard $\mathrm{argmax}$. At equal scores, probability is spread uniformly. This smooth, differentiable interpolation between hard selection and uniform spread is why the function is called softmax.

Softmax Prediction
$$p(y=j \mid x;\Theta) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j^\top x)}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^k \exp(\theta_\ell^\top x)}$$

6.6.2 Geometric Interpretation

The geometry of softmax regression generalizes the two-class picture. In logistic regression, one vector $\theta$ defines a separating hyperplane $\theta^\top x = 0$; points on one side are positive, the other negative. In softmax regression there is one vector $\theta_j$ per class. The score for class $j$ at input $x$ is $\theta_j^\top x$, proportional to the projection of $x$ onto $\theta_j$. A point is classified as class $j$ when $x$ is most aligned with $\theta_j$ — when the dot product $\theta_j^\top x$ exceeds all others. The decision boundaries are piecewise linear hyperplanes dividing the input space into $k$ polyhedral regions.

Figure 6.6. Left: geometric interpretation with $k=3$ classes. One parameter vector $\theta_k$ points toward each cluster (arrows from origin). A new point $x$ is classified as the class whose $\theta_k$ is most aligned with $x$ (largest dot product). Right: example raw scores $[2.1, 0.3, -0.8]$ (lighter bars) converted to softmax probabilities (darker bars) for the three classes. Exponentiation amplifies the score gap; renormalization yields valid probabilities approximately $[0.84, 0.12, 0.04]$.
Warning · Parameter Redundancy in Softmax

The softmax model with $k$ parameter vectors has a structural redundancy: subtracting any fixed vector $v$ from all $\theta_j$ simultaneously leaves every predicted probability unchanged, since the $e^{v^\top x}$ factors cancel. The model therefore has only $(k-1)d$ effective degrees of freedom, not $kd$. In practice this is handled by $L_2$ regularization (which implicitly anchors $\theta$ near zero) or by fixing $\theta_k = \mathbf{0}$ and treating class $k$ as the reference. For $k=2$ with $\theta_2 = \mathbf{0}$, softmax reduces exactly to logistic regression with parameter $\theta_1$ — as the reader should verify.

Data Science Application · Softmax as a Neural Network Output Layer

In deep learning, softmax regression is universally used as the final layer of a classification network. The penultimate layer produces a vector of "logits" $z = W^\top h \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (where $h$ is the learned representation); softmax converts these to class probabilities. Training minimizes the cross-entropy loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^n \log p(y^{(i)} \mid x^{(i)};\Theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^k \mathbf{1}[y^{(i)}=j]\log p(y=j \mid x^{(i)};\Theta),$$

which is exactly the negative log-likelihood of the categorical GLM. During backpropagation, the gradient with respect to the logits is $\hat{p} - e_{y^{(i)}}$ (predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label) — the GLM update rule in disguise. The exponential family structure underlies every modern image classifier.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter developed the exponential family and Generalized Linear Models as a unified probabilistic framework for supervised learning. We began with the canonical form $p(y;\eta)=b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y)-a(\eta))$ and used exponential tilting to explain where this form originates. We then derived the exponential family representations of Bernoulli and Gaussian through pattern-matching, recovering the logistic sigmoid as a mathematical necessity rather than a design choice. The key property — that $a'(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[y]$ and $a''(\eta)=\mathrm{Var}[y]$ — unifies moment computation and implies convexity of the MLE. The three GLM assumptions connect linear predictors to any exponential family, yielding a universal gradient update rule. Softmax regression then extended the framework to multi-class classification via the categorical exponential family, with the same cross-entropy loss structure used in all modern neural network classifiers.

EXPONENTIAL FAMILY FORM

$p(y;\eta)=b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y)-a(\eta))$. The four components are base measure $b(y)$, sufficient statistic $T(y)$, natural parameter $\eta$, and log-partition $a(\eta)$. The class includes Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, gamma, and many others.

EXPONENTIAL TILTING

The family arises by multiplying a base measure $b(y)$ by $e^{\eta y}$ and renormalizing. The denominator's log becomes $a(\eta)$. This "tilts" mass toward high or low $y$ based on the sign of $\eta$, and the log-partition tracks the normalizing cost as $\eta$ varies.

BERNOULLI FAMILY

Natural parameter $\eta=\log(\phi/(1-\phi))$; log-partition $a(\eta)=\log(1+e^\eta)$. The inversion $\phi=\sigma(\eta)$ reveals the logistic sigmoid as the canonical response function, not a heuristic choice. Base measure $b(y)=1$.

GAUSSIAN FAMILY

Natural parameter $\eta=\mu$; log-partition $a(\eta)=\eta^2/2$. The canonical response is the identity $g(\eta)=\eta$, leading directly to linear regression. The base measure is the standard normal density.

MOMENT PROPERTIES OF $a(\eta)$

$\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]=a'(\eta)$ and $\mathrm{Var}[y;\eta]=a''(\eta)$. Proved by differentiating the normalization identity. Implies that (1) moments are computed by differentiation rather than integration, and (2) $a$ is convex (variance $\geq 0$), so the negative log-likelihood is convex.

THREE GLM ASSUMPTIONS

(1) $y|x \sim \mathrm{ExpFamily}(\eta)$; (2) $h_\theta(x)=\mathbb{E}[y|x;\theta]$; (3) $\eta=\theta^\top x$. Together they force $h_\theta(x)=g(\theta^\top x)$ where $g=a'$ is the canonical response function.

CANONICAL RESPONSE FUNCTION

$g(\eta)=a'(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ maps natural to mean parameter. Identity for Gaussian; sigmoid for Bernoulli; exponential for Poisson. Always invertible (canonical link $g^{-1}$) because $a$ is strictly convex.

UNIVERSAL UPDATE RULE

$\theta:=\theta+\alpha(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)}))x^{(i)}$ holds for all GLMs. The error signal is always "observed minus predicted mean." Proved in one line from the moment property $a'(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ and the chain rule.

POISSON REGRESSION

Natural parameter $\eta=\log\lambda$; log-partition $a(\eta)=e^\eta$; canonical response $g(\eta)=e^\eta$. Hypothesis: $h_\theta(x)=e^{\theta^\top x}>0$. Always predicts positive values, consistent with count data. Coefficients have multiplicative (not additive) interpretations.

SOFTMAX REGRESSION

Categorical GLM for $k$-class output: $p(y=j|x)=e^{\theta_j^\top x}/\sum_\ell e^{\theta_\ell^\top x}$. One $\theta_j$ per class. For $k=2$ with $\theta_2=0$, reduces to logistic regression. The cross-entropy loss is the categorical GLM's negative log-likelihood; the backprop gradient is $\hat{p}-e_y$.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 · Exponential Family Derivation
Deriving the Poisson Distribution's Exponential Family Form

(a) Starting from $p(y;\lambda) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y/y!$ for $y \in \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, perform the algebraic derivation to express it in exponential family form. Identify $b(y)$, $T(y)$, $\eta$, and $a(\eta)$ explicitly, showing all steps.

(b) Using the moment properties of the exponential family, compute $\mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ and $\mathrm{Var}[y;\eta]$ by differentiating $a(\eta)$. Verify that these match the known Poisson moments (mean = variance = $\lambda$).

(c) Explain why $\mathrm{Var}[y]=\mathbb{E}[y]$ for Poisson in terms of the exponential family structure: what property of $a(\eta)=e^\eta$ implies equidispersion? For which other exponential family distributions does $a''(\eta) = a'(\eta)$?

(d) Data science extension: After fitting a Poisson GLM to website log data you compute sample mean $\bar{y} = 12.3$ and sample variance $s^2 = 47.8$ on held-out data. What does this suggest about your model assumptions? Name a more flexible distribution you could use, explain what additional parameter it introduces, and describe how you would check whether the additional flexibility is warranted.

Exercise 6.2 · Moment Properties
Proving Mean and Variance from the Log-Partition Function

(a) Prove rigorously that $\mathbb{E}[y;\eta] = a'(\eta)$ for a scalar exponential family distribution with $T(y)=y$. Start from the normalization identity $\int p(y;\eta)\,dy=1$, differentiate with respect to $\eta$, and clearly state any regularity conditions required for differentiation under the integral sign.

(b) Extend to prove $\mathrm{Var}[y;\eta] = a''(\eta)$ by differentiating the result from (a) a second time. Show all intermediate steps and identify where the definition of variance is used.

(c) Use part (b) to prove that $a(\eta)$ is convex in $\eta$ for any exponential family distribution with non-degenerate variance. Conclude that the log-likelihood $\ell(\eta) = \log p(y;\eta)$ is concave in $\eta$.

(d) Data science extension: A practitioner claims "the exponential family log-likelihood is concave, so gradient descent always converges to the global maximum." Identify one important caveat: the concavity guarantee is in $\eta$, but in a GLM you optimize over $\theta$ with $\eta = \theta^\top x$. Explain why concavity in $\eta$ implies concavity in $\theta$ for a GLM, and state the key linear-algebra property of the composition that preserves convexity.

Exercise 6.3 · GLM Construction
Building a Gamma GLM for Positive Real-Valued Insurance Claim Amounts

(a) The Gamma distribution with fixed shape $k>0$ and rate parameter $r>0$ has pdf $p(y;k,r) = \frac{r^k}{\Gamma(k)}y^{k-1}e^{-ry}$ for $y>0$. Treating $r$ as the varying parameter, write the Gamma pdf in exponential family form. Identify $\eta$, $a(\eta)$, $b(y)$, $T(y)$.

(b) Derive the canonical response function $g(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ for the Gamma family. Show that $g(\eta) = -k/\eta$ (noting $\eta = -r < 0$). Derive the canonical link $g^{-1}(\mu) = -k/\mu$.

(c) Construct the Gamma GLM using the three assumptions with $\eta = \theta^\top x$. Write down $h_\theta(x)$ and state the constraint on $\theta^\top x$ needed for a valid prediction. What happens if $\theta^\top x \geq 0$?

(d) Data science extension: You are modeling insurance claim amounts (strictly positive continuous values). Compare the Gamma GLM with a Gaussian GLM for this task. What goes wrong with Gaussian predictions when $\theta^\top x$ is small? In practice, why is the Gamma GLM better calibrated for the heavy right tail typically observed in insurance losses?

Exercise 6.4 · Universal Update Rule
Deriving the Gradient Update for Logistic and Poisson Regression

(a) Derive the gradient update rule for logistic regression from first principles. Write the Bernoulli log-likelihood $\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \log p(y^{(i)};\sigma(\theta^\top x^{(i)}))$, compute $\partial\ell/\partial\theta_j$, and simplify to the form $(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)}))x_j^{(i)}$. You may use $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$.

(b) Repeat part (a) for the Poisson GLM with $h_\theta(x) = e^{\theta^\top x}$. Derive the update rule from the Poisson log-likelihood and confirm it takes the same universal form.

(c) Argue from the exponential family structure (without computing specific derivatives) why the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta_j$ must always equal $(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)}))x_j^{(i)}$. Your argument should reference the moment property $a'(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[y;\eta]$ and the chain rule with $\eta = \theta^\top x$.

(d) Data science extension: In mini-batch gradient descent you average the update over a batch $\mathcal{B}$ of size $B$. For a Poisson GLM on count data, explain how a single example with an unusually large count $y^{(i)} \gg \hat{y}^{(i)}$ can produce an extremely large gradient step. Name two practical strategies to mitigate this instability in Poisson regression training.

Exercise 6.5 · Softmax Regression
Reducing Softmax to Logistic Regression and Deriving the Cross-Entropy Gradient

(a) Show that softmax regression with $k=2$ classes, with $\theta_2 = \mathbf{0}$, reduces exactly to logistic regression. Derive $p(y=1|x;\theta_1,\mathbf{0})$ explicitly and show it equals $\sigma(\theta_1^\top x)$.

(b) For softmax regression with $k$ classes, the log-likelihood for one example is $\ell = \sum_j \mathbf{1}[y=j]\log p(y=j|x;\Theta)$ (cross-entropy). Derive $\partial\ell/\partial\theta_j$ for the correct class $j = y^{(i)}$ and show it equals $(1 - p(y=j|x))x^{(i)}$.

(c) Derive the gradient for an incorrect class $\ell \neq y^{(i)}$ and show it equals $-p(y=\ell|x)x^{(i)}$. Verify that the sum over all classes $\sum_j \partial\ell/\partial\theta_j = \mathbf{0}$, reflecting the softmax normalization constraint.

(d) Data science extension: Computing $\exp(\theta_j^\top x)$ can overflow for large logits. Prove the identity $\log\sum_j e^{z_j} = c + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - c}$ for any scalar $c$, and show that choosing $c = \max_j z_j$ ensures all arguments of exp are $\leq 0$ (preventing overflow). Write pseudocode for a numerically stable softmax implementation using this log-sum-exp trick.
